title: Waves
description: Waves — Class 11 Physics (NCERT): transverse & longitudinal waves, wave speed v=fλ, progressive wave equation, waves on a string, superposition, standing waves, beats & the Doppler effect, with solved numericals & tests.

topics.title: Nature & Types of Waves
topics.concept:
A wave is a disturbance that travels through a medium, carrying energy and momentum from one place to another without any bulk movement of the medium itself. When you drop a stone in a pond, the ripples spread outward, but a floating leaf only bobs up and down — it does not travel with the ripple. That single observation captures the heart of wave motion: the pattern moves, the particles do not.

Mechanical waves need a material medium (solid, liquid or gas) to travel through, because they rely on the elasticity and inertia of the medium. Sound, water ripples and waves on a string are all mechanical. They cannot travel through a vacuum — which is why no one can hear an explosion in outer space. (Electromagnetic waves like light need no medium, but in Class 11 we focus on mechanical waves.)

Mechanical waves come in two kinds, classified by the direction in which particles vibrate relative to the direction the wave travels:

  • Transverse waves: particles of the medium vibrate perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation. A wave on a stretched string is transverse — you shake the end up and down, but the pulse runs along the string. Transverse waves show crests (high points) and troughs (low points). They can travel through solids and on liquid surfaces, but not through the body of a gas or liquid.
  • Longitudinal waves: particles vibrate parallel to the direction of propagation. Sound in air is longitudinal — the air is alternately squeezed and stretched, forming regions of compression (high pressure) and rarefaction (low pressure). These can travel through solids, liquids and gases.

Wave parameters. Any periodic wave is described by a few key quantities:

  • Wavelength $\lambda$: the distance between two consecutive identical points (crest to crest, or compression to compression), measured in metres.
  • Frequency $f$: the number of complete oscillations per second, in hertz (Hz). The time period $T=\frac{1}{f}$ is the time for one full oscillation.
  • Amplitude $A$: the maximum displacement of a particle from its rest position.
  • Wave speed $v$: how fast the disturbance travels. The fundamental relation is $v=f\lambda$.

A travelling (progressive) wave moving in the $+x$ direction is written as $y=A\sin(\omega t-kx)$, where $\omega=2\pi f$ is the angular frequency and $k=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}$ is the angular wave number. From these, $v=\frac{\omega}{k}=f\lambda$.

The speed of a wave depends only on the medium, not on the frequency. On a stretched string of tension $T$ and linear mass density $\mu$ (mass per unit length), the speed is $v=\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$. For sound, the speed depends on the elasticity and density of the medium: it is fastest in solids (about 5000 m/s in steel), slower in liquids (about 1500 m/s in water) and slowest in gases (about 340 m/s in air at room temperature).

examples.problem: A wave has a frequency of 500 Hz and a wavelength of 0.68 m. Calculate its speed.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Use $v=f\lambda$.
  2. Step 2: Substitute: $v=500\times0.68$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $v=340\ \text{m/s}$.

Answer: $v=340\ \text{m/s}$ (the speed of sound in air).

examples.problem: A radio station broadcasts at a frequency of 100 MHz. Find the wavelength of the waves. (Speed of EM waves $=3\times10^{8}\ \text{m/s}$.)
A string of mass 5 g and length 1 m is stretched with a tension of 80 N. Find the speed of a transverse wave on it.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Linear mass density $\mu=\frac{m}{L}=\frac{5\times10^{-3}}{1}=5\times10^{-3}\ \text{kg/m}$.
  2. Step 2: Use $v=\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}=\sqrt{\frac{80}{5\times10^{-3}}}=\sqrt{1.6\times10^{4}}$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $v=126\ \text{m/s}$.

Answer: $v\approx126\ \text{m/s}$.

examples.problem: A progressive wave is given by $y=0.02\sin(300t-2x)$ (SI units). Find its amplitude, angular frequency, wave number, wavelength and speed.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Compare with $y=A\sin(\omega t-kx)$: amplitude $A=0.02\ \text{m}$, $\omega=300\ \text{rad/s}$, $k=2\ \text{rad/m}$.
  2. Step 2: Wavelength $\lambda=\frac{2\pi}{k}=\frac{2\pi}{2}=\pi\approx3.14\ \text{m}$.
  3. Step 3: Speed $v=\frac{\omega}{k}=\frac{300}{2}=150\ \text{m/s}$.

Answer: $A=0.02\ \text{m}$, $\omega=300\ \text{rad/s}$, $k=2\ \text{rad/m}$, $\lambda\approx3.14\ \text{m}$, $v=150\ \text{m/s}$.

examples.problem: The time period of a wave is 0.004 s and its speed is 350 m/s. Find its frequency and wavelength.
The tension in a string is increased four times without changing anything else. How does the speed of a transverse wave on it change?
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Since $v=\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$, we have $v\propto\sqrt{T}$.
  2. Step 2: Replacing $T$ by $4T$: $v'\propto\sqrt{4T}=2\sqrt{T}$.
  3. Step 3: Therefore $v'=2v$.

Answer: The wave speed doubles.

recap: A wave transports energy and momentum through a medium without bulk transport of the medium; mechanical waves need a material medium.
Transverse waves: particles vibrate perpendicular to propagation (crests & troughs); longitudinal waves: particles vibrate parallel (compressions & rarefactions).
Key relation: $v=f\lambda$, with $\omega=2\pi f$ and $k=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}$; a progressive wave is $y=A\sin(\omega t-kx)$.
Speed of a transverse wave on a string: $v=\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$, where $\mu$ is the linear mass density.
Wave speed depends on the medium, not on the frequency; sound is fastest in solids, slowest in gases.

quiz.q: In a longitudinal wave, the particles of the medium vibrate:
options: perpendicular to the direction of propagation
parallel to the direction of propagation
quiz.explanation: Longitudinal waves (like sound) have particle vibrations parallel to the wave's travel, forming compressions and rarefactions.

quiz.q: The relation between wave speed, frequency and wavelength is:
quiz.explanation: A wave travels one wavelength in one time period, so $v=\frac{\lambda}{T}=f\lambda$.

quiz.q: The speed of a transverse wave on a stretched string is given by:
quiz.explanation: Wave speed on a string is $v=\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$, where $T$ is tension and $\mu$ is mass per unit length.
Sound is a mechanical wave and needs a material medium; it cannot travel through a vacuum.

topics.title: Superposition & Standing Waves
topics.concept:
What happens when two waves arrive at the same point at the same time? The principle of superposition answers this: when two or more waves overlap, the resultant displacement at any point is the vector sum of the individual displacements. The waves pass through each other and emerge unchanged — they do not collide or scatter. This single principle underlies interference, beats and standing waves.

Interference is the result of superposing two waves of the same frequency travelling in the same direction:

  • Constructive interference occurs when the waves arrive in phase (crest meets crest). The amplitudes add, giving a louder sound or brighter light. This needs a path difference of a whole number of wavelengths: $\Delta x=n\lambda$.
  • Destructive interference occurs when the waves arrive out of phase by half a cycle (crest meets trough). The amplitudes cancel, giving silence or darkness. This needs a path difference of an odd number of half-wavelengths: $\Delta x=(2n+1)\frac{\lambda}{2}$.

Reflection of waves. When a wave hits a boundary it is reflected. The nature of the reflection depends on the boundary:

  • At a rigid (fixed) boundary, the reflected wave suffers a phase change of $\pi$ (a crest returns as a trough). A node always forms there.
  • At a free (open) boundary, the reflected wave has no phase change. An antinode forms there.

Standing (stationary) waves form when two identical waves travel in opposite directions and superpose — typically an incident wave and its reflection. The result is a pattern that appears to stand still: $y=2A\sin(kx)\cos(\omega t)$. Energy is not transported along the medium; it stays trapped. The pattern has:

  • Nodes: points of zero displacement (always at rest). Spacing between consecutive nodes is $\frac{\lambda}{2}$.
  • Antinodes: points of maximum displacement (vibrating most). They lie midway between nodes.

Standing waves on a string fixed at both ends (length $L$): both ends must be nodes, so only certain wavelengths fit. The allowed frequencies are $f_n=\frac{n}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$ for $n=1,2,3,\dots$ The lowest is the fundamental (first harmonic), $f_1=\frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$, and the higher ones ($2f_1, 3f_1, \dots$) are harmonics. An overtone is any frequency above the fundamental; the first overtone is the second harmonic.

Air columns. Wind instruments use standing waves of sound:

  • An open pipe (open at both ends) has antinodes at both ends. It produces all harmonics: $f_n=\frac{nv}{2L}$ ($n=1,2,3,\dots$).
  • A closed pipe (one end closed) has a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end. It produces only odd harmonics: $f_n=\frac{nv}{4L}$ ($n=1,3,5,\dots$). Its fundamental is $\frac{v}{4L}$ — half the open pipe's, which is why a closed pipe of the same length sounds an octave lower.

examples.problem: A string fixed at both ends is 0.5 m long and a transverse wave travels on it at 100 m/s. Find the fundamental frequency.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: For a string fixed at both ends, $f_1=\frac{v}{2L}$.
  2. Step 2: Substitute: $f_1=\frac{100}{2\times0.5}=\frac{100}{1}$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $f_1=100\ \text{Hz}$.

Answer: Fundamental frequency $f_1=100\ \text{Hz}$.

examples.problem: An open pipe of length 0.34 m resonates with air. Find its fundamental frequency. (Speed of sound $=340\ \text{m/s}$.)
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: For an open pipe, $f_1=\frac{v}{2L}$.
  2. Step 2: Substitute: $f_1=\frac{340}{2\times0.34}=\frac{340}{0.68}$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $f_1=500\ \text{Hz}$.

Answer: $f_1=500\ \text{Hz}$.

examples.problem: A closed pipe of length 0.34 m is sounded. Find its fundamental frequency. (Speed of sound $=340\ \text{m/s}$.)
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: For a pipe closed at one end, $f_1=\frac{v}{4L}$.
  2. Step 2: Substitute: $f_1=\frac{340}{4\times0.34}=\frac{340}{1.36}$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $f_1=250\ \text{Hz}$ — exactly half that of an open pipe of the same length.

Answer: $f_1=250\ \text{Hz}$.

examples.problem: Two waves of equal amplitude interfere. Find the resultant amplitude when they are (a) in phase and (b) exactly out of phase, with each amplitude $A$.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: For in-phase (constructive) superposition, amplitudes add: $A_{res}=A+A=2A$.
  2. Step 2: For out-of-phase (destructive) superposition, amplitudes subtract: $A_{res}=A-A=0$.
  3. Step 3: So intensity (proportional to amplitude squared) is $4$ times one wave when constructive, and zero when destructive.

Answer: (a) $2A$ (constructive); (b) $0$ (destructive).

examples.problem: The first overtone of a string fixed at both ends is 240 Hz. What is its fundamental frequency?
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: For a string fixed at both ends, all harmonics are present: $f_n=nf_1$.
  2. Step 2: The first overtone is the second harmonic, so $f_2=2f_1=240\ \text{Hz}$.
  3. Step 3: Therefore $f_1=\frac{240}{2}=120\ \text{Hz}$.

Answer: Fundamental frequency $=120\ \text{Hz}$.

examples.problem: A closed pipe has a fundamental frequency of 200 Hz. Find the frequency of its first overtone.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: A closed pipe produces only odd harmonics: $f_1, 3f_1, 5f_1,\dots$
  2. Step 2: The first overtone is the next allowed mode, the third harmonic: $f=3f_1$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $f=3\times200=600\ \text{Hz}$.

Answer: First overtone $=600\ \text{Hz}$ (the third harmonic).

recap: Principle of superposition: the resultant displacement is the vector sum of the individual wave displacements.
Constructive interference (in phase, $\Delta x=n\lambda$) adds amplitudes; destructive ($\Delta x=(2n+1)\frac{\lambda}{2}$) cancels them.
Standing waves form from two opposite-travelling waves: $y=2A\sin(kx)\cos(\omega t)$; nodes are at rest, antinodes vibrate most, node spacing is $\frac{\lambda}{2}$.
String fixed at both ends and an open pipe give all harmonics; a closed pipe gives only odd harmonics ($f_1=\frac{v}{4L}$).
The first overtone is the second harmonic for a string/open pipe, but the third harmonic for a closed pipe.

quiz.q: When two waves arrive at a point exactly out of phase, the interference is:
quiz.explanation: Out-of-phase waves (crest meets trough) cancel, giving destructive interference.

quiz.q: In a standing wave, the distance between two consecutive nodes is:
quiz.explanation: Nodes occur every half wavelength, so consecutive nodes are $\frac{\lambda}{2}$ apart.

quiz.q: A pipe closed at one end produces only:
quiz.explanation: A closed pipe has a node at the closed end and antinode at the open end, allowing only odd harmonics ($f_n=\frac{nv}{4L}$, $n$ odd).

quiz.q: The fundamental frequency of a string fixed at both ends of length $L$ is:
quiz.explanation: Both ends are nodes, so $L=\frac{\lambda}{2}$ for the fundamental, giving $f_1=\frac{v}{2L}$.

topics.title: Beats & the Doppler Effect
topics.concept:
So far we have superposed waves of the same frequency. What if the two frequencies differ slightly? The answer is one of the most useful effects in acoustics: beats.

Beats are the periodic rise and fall in the loudness of sound heard when two notes of slightly different frequencies are sounded together. At some instants the two waves are in phase and reinforce (loud); a moment later they slip out of phase and cancel (soft). One loud–soft cycle is one beat.

  • Beat frequency $=|f_1-f_2|$ — the number of beats heard per second equals the difference of the two frequencies.
  • Beats are clearly audible only when the difference is small (roughly up to 6–7 Hz); beyond that the ear cannot resolve the separate loud–soft cycles.
  • Beats are the basis of tuning: a musician adjusts an instrument against a reference until the beats slow down and vanish, meaning the frequencies match exactly.

For example, two tuning forks of 256 Hz and 260 Hz sounded together produce $|260-256|=4$ beats per second.

The Doppler effect is the apparent change in the frequency (pitch) of a sound when there is relative motion between the source and the observer. You hear it every day: the pitch of an approaching ambulance siren is higher than its true pitch, and it suddenly drops to a lower pitch as the ambulance passes and recedes.

The general formula for the observed frequency $f'$ when the source emits frequency $f$ in still air of sound speed $v$ is:

  • $f'=f\left(\frac{v\pm v_o}{v\mp v_s}\right)$, where $v_o$ is the observer's speed and $v_s$ is the source's speed.
  • Sign convention: choose the signs so that motion of either body towards the other raises $f'$, and motion away lowers it. Use the upper sign in the numerator ($+v_o$) when the observer moves towards the source; use the upper sign in the denominator ($-v_s$) when the source moves towards the observer.

Some standard cases (sound speed $v$):

  • Source approaching, observer at rest: $f'=f\left(\frac{v}{v-v_s}\right)$ — pitch rises.
  • Source receding, observer at rest: $f'=f\left(\frac{v}{v+v_s}\right)$ — pitch falls.
  • Observer approaching, source at rest: $f'=f\left(\frac{v+v_o}{v}\right)$ — pitch rises.

Note that the Doppler effect for sound is not symmetric in $v_o$ and $v_s$ — a moving source and a moving observer at the same speed give slightly different shifts, because sound travels in a medium (air) which provides a frame of reference. Applications include speed-detecting radar guns used by traffic police, weather radar for storms, medical ultrasound to measure blood flow, and sonar for detecting submarines. Astronomers use the Doppler shift of starlight (red shift) as evidence that the universe is expanding.

examples.problem: Two tuning forks of frequencies 480 Hz and 484 Hz are sounded together. Find the beat frequency.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Beat frequency $=|f_1-f_2|$.
  2. Step 2: Substitute: $=|484-480|$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $=4\ \text{Hz}$ (4 beats per second).

Answer: Beat frequency $=4\ \text{Hz}$.

examples.problem: A tuning fork of unknown frequency gives 5 beats per second with a 256 Hz fork. On loading the unknown fork with wax, the beat frequency drops to 3 per second. Find the unknown frequency.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: The unknown frequency is either $256+5=261$ Hz or $256-5=251$ Hz.
  2. Step 2: Loading with wax lowers the unknown fork's frequency. If it were 261 Hz, lowering it towards 256 would reduce beats — consistent with the drop to 3.
  3. Step 3: If it were 251 Hz, lowering it further would increase the beats (to more than 5), which contradicts the observation. So the unknown frequency is 261 Hz.

Answer: The unknown frequency is $261\ \text{Hz}$.

examples.problem: A source of frequency 500 Hz moves towards a stationary observer at 30 m/s. Find the observed frequency. (Speed of sound $=330\ \text{m/s}$.)
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Source approaching, observer at rest: $f'=f\left(\frac{v}{v-v_s}\right)$.
  2. Step 2: Substitute: $f'=500\left(\frac{330}{330-30}\right)=500\left(\frac{330}{300}\right)$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $f'=500\times1.1=550\ \text{Hz}$.

Answer: $f'=550\ \text{Hz}$ (pitch rises).

examples.problem: The same 500 Hz source now moves away from the stationary observer at 30 m/s. Find the observed frequency. (Speed of sound $=330\ \text{m/s}$.)
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Source receding, observer at rest: $f'=f\left(\frac{v}{v+v_s}\right)$.
  2. Step 2: Substitute: $f'=500\left(\frac{330}{330+30}\right)=500\left(\frac{330}{360}\right)$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $f'=500\times0.9167\approx458\ \text{Hz}$.

Answer: $f'\approx458\ \text{Hz}$ (pitch falls).

examples.problem: An observer moves towards a stationary source of frequency 400 Hz at 33 m/s. Find the observed frequency. (Speed of sound $=330\ \text{m/s}$.)
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Observer approaching, source at rest: $f'=f\left(\frac{v+v_o}{v}\right)$.
  2. Step 2: Substitute: $f'=400\left(\frac{330+33}{330}\right)=400\left(\frac{363}{330}\right)$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $f'=400\times1.1=440\ \text{Hz}$.

Answer: $f'=440\ \text{Hz}$.

examples.problem: A car sounding a horn of 600 Hz approaches a stationary listener at 20 m/s. Find the frequency heard. (Speed of sound $=340\ \text{m/s}$.)
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Source approaching, observer at rest: $f'=f\left(\frac{v}{v-v_s}\right)$.
  2. Step 2: Substitute: $f'=600\left(\frac{340}{340-20}\right)=600\left(\frac{340}{320}\right)$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $f'=600\times1.0625=637.5\ \text{Hz}$.

Answer: $f'\approx637.5\ \text{Hz}$.

recap: Beats arise from superposing two waves of slightly different frequencies; beat frequency $=|f_1-f_2|$.
Beats are audible only for small frequency differences (about 6–7 Hz) and are used to tune instruments to a reference.
The Doppler effect is the apparent change in pitch due to relative motion of source and observer: $f'=f\left(\frac{v\pm v_o}{v\mp v_s}\right)$.
Motion towards raises the observed frequency; motion away lowers it; the effect is not symmetric in $v_o$ and $v_s$ for sound.
Applications: radar speed guns, weather radar, medical ultrasound, sonar, and astronomical red shift.

quiz.q: The beat frequency produced by two tuning forks of frequencies $f_1$ and $f_2$ is:
quiz.explanation: The number of beats per second equals the magnitude of the difference of the two frequencies, $|f_1-f_2|$.

quiz.q: When a source of sound moves towards a stationary observer, the observed frequency:
quiz.explanation: Wavefronts bunch up ahead of the approaching source, so the observed frequency (pitch) rises: $f'=f\frac{v}{v-v_s}$.

quiz.q: Beats can be heard clearly only when the two frequencies differ by:
quiz.explanation: The ear can resolve separate loud–soft cycles only when the difference is small, roughly up to 6–7 Hz.

quiz.q: The Doppler effect is used in all of the following EXCEPT:
quiz.explanation: Tuning a guitar by ear uses beats, not the Doppler effect; the other three rely on Doppler frequency shifts.

questions.q: A wave carries from one place to another:
questions.explanation: A wave transports energy and momentum through the medium without bulk movement of the medium itself.

questions.q: Which of the following is a longitudinal wave?
questions.explanation: Sound in air is longitudinal — air particles vibrate parallel to the direction of propagation.

questions.q: The relation $v=f\lambda$ holds because in one time period the wave advances by:
questions.explanation: The wave moves one wavelength in one period $T$, so $v=\frac{\lambda}{T}=f\lambda$.

questions.q: The speed of a transverse wave on a string of tension $T$ and mass per unit length $\mu$ is:
questions.explanation: Wave speed on a string is $v=\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$.

questions.q: A wave of frequency 200 Hz travels at 360 m/s. Its wavelength is:
questions.explanation: $\lambda=\frac{v}{f}=\frac{360}{200}=1.8\ \text{m}$.

questions.q: In $y=A\sin(\omega t-kx)$, the wave speed equals:
questions.explanation: Wave speed $v=\frac{\omega}{k}=f\lambda$.

questions.q: If the tension in a string is made 9 times, the wave speed becomes:
questions.explanation: $v\propto\sqrt{T}$, so $\sqrt{9}=3$; the speed triples.

questions.q: The principle of superposition states that the resultant displacement is the:
questions.explanation: Overlapping waves add by vector sum of displacements.

questions.q: Constructive interference occurs when the path difference is:
questions.explanation: In-phase waves (path difference a whole number of wavelengths, $n\lambda$) reinforce.

questions.q: In a standing wave, points of zero displacement are called:
questions.explanation: Nodes are points that remain permanently at rest in a standing wave.

questions.q: The distance between a node and the next antinode is:
questions.explanation: Node-to-antinode spacing is a quarter wavelength, $\frac{\lambda}{4}$.

questions.q: A pipe closed at one end produces:
questions.explanation: A closed pipe (node at closed end, antinode at open end) gives only odd harmonics, $f_n=\frac{nv}{4L}$, $n$ odd.

questions.q: The fundamental frequency of an open pipe of length $L$ is:
questions.explanation: An open pipe has antinodes at both ends, $L=\frac{\lambda}{2}$, so $f_1=\frac{v}{2L}$.

questions.q: Two forks of 256 Hz and 260 Hz sounded together give beats per second:
questions.explanation: Beat frequency $=|260-256|=4\ \text{Hz}$.

questions.q: Beats are used mainly to:
questions.explanation: Beats vanish when two frequencies match, so they let a musician tune an instrument precisely.

questions.q: The Doppler effect is the apparent change in the sound's:
questions.explanation: Relative motion of source and observer changes the observed frequency (pitch).

questions.q: A source of 500 Hz approaches a stationary observer at 33 m/s ($v=330$ m/s). The observed frequency is about:
When a sound source moves away from a stationary observer, the observed pitch:
questions.explanation: Receding source: $f'=f\frac{v}{v+v_s}<f$, so the pitch falls.

questions.q: A string under tension $T$ has wave speed $v$. To double $v$, the tension must be made:
questions.explanation: $v\propto\sqrt{T}$, so doubling $v$ needs $T$ to be quadrupled.

questions.q: A closed pipe and an open pipe have the same fundamental frequency. The ratio of their lengths (closed:open) is:
questions.explanation: Closed $f_1=\frac{v}{4L_c}$, open $f_1=\frac{v}{2L_o}$; equal $\Rightarrow\frac{v}{4L_c}=\frac{v}{2L_o}\Rightarrow L_c=\frac{L_o}{2}$, ratio 1:2.

questions.q: The first overtone of a closed pipe has the same frequency as the fundamental of an open pipe. The ratio of their lengths (closed:open) is:
questions.explanation: Closed first overtone $=\frac{3v}{4L_c}$; open fundamental $=\frac{v}{2L_o}$. Equal $\Rightarrow\frac{3}{4L_c}=\frac{1}{2L_o}\Rightarrow L_c=\frac{3L_o}{2}$, ratio 3:2.

questions.q: Two strings of the same material and length have radii in ratio 1:2 under the same tension. The ratio of their fundamental frequencies is:
questions.explanation: $\mu\propto r^2$ and $f\propto\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu}}\propto\frac{1}{r}$, so $f_1:f_2=r_2:r_1=2:1$.

questions.q: A tuning fork gives 4 beats/s with a 320 Hz fork. After filing the tuning fork, the beats become 6/s. The original frequency of the filed fork was:
questions.explanation: Filing raises a fork's frequency. Beats increased, so the fork was below 320 (316 Hz); filing raised it further from 320 (316→above), increasing beats.

questions.q: A wave $y=A\sin(\omega t-kx)$ meets a rigid wall and reflects. The reflected wave is:
questions.explanation: Reflection at a rigid boundary reverses direction and adds a phase change of $\pi$, giving $-A\sin(\omega t+kx)$.

questions.q: A source and an observer both move towards each other at speed $u$ ($v=$ sound speed). The observed frequency is:
questions.explanation: Observer towards (+$u$ in numerator), source towards ($-u$ in denominator): $f'=f\frac{v+u}{v-u}$.

questions.q: A car moving at $v_s$ towards a wall sounds a horn of frequency $f$. The beat frequency between the direct horn and the echo heard by the driver is largest when $v_s$ is:
questions.explanation: Beats arise only when the car moves; the echo is Doppler-shifted, so a nonzero (and increasing) $v_s$ gives audible, growing beats.

questions.q: If the speed of sound increases with temperature, the fundamental frequency of an open pipe on a hot day will:
questions.explanation: $f_1=\frac{v}{2L}$; a higher $v$ (warmer air) raises the fundamental frequency.

questions.q: The number of beats heard per second when 500 Hz and 506 Hz are sounded together, and the maximum loudness occurs at intervals of:
questions.explanation: Beat frequency $=|506-500|=6$ Hz, so maxima recur every $\frac{1}{6}$ s.

questions.q: In a stationary wave on a string, the energy:
options: is not transported but remains confined
questions.explanation: A standing wave transports no net energy; it remains confined between the fixed boundaries.

questions.q: A whistle of frequency $f$ is whirled in a horizontal circle. A distant observer hears a frequency that:
options: varies between a maximum and a minimum about $f$
questions.explanation: As the source alternately approaches and recedes along the line of sight, the Doppler-shifted frequency oscillates above and below $f$.
